utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, would the witness take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Moroz.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D26251 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you remember having given this testimony before this Tribunal and in the Galic case? We can see the transcript of that testimony on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: So yes I did -- I provided some information during the Galic Tribunal -- the Galic case, and so I have a chance to look through during several days this transcription I got from Mr. Robinson, and I should say that everything I testified I consider it truth and I was frank 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I put the same questions to you as the questions that were put to you when you testified in this case, would the answers you provide be the same answers that we can see in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could I tender this transcript into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter, part of a package and with an associated document, the nature of which will be explained to you by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning. No, Your Honours, except that there is a procedural matter unrelated to the witness at transcript pages 18194, line 7, to 18203, line 5, which may be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We'll take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it to the parties. This will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 1D26251 will be Exhibit D2373.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, if we could call up 1D25442. This is listed as an additional exhibit with this witness and the Prosecution has agreed that this document can be admitted, so I would just like to read it and then Dr. Karadzic can read the summary of the testimony of this witness. This document is a letter that was sent to me by the Russian embassy and it pertains to a person who Colonel Moroz will be relating a conversation that he had with. And it says that according to the data of the Ministry of Defence of Russia, Nikolay Vasilievich Rumyantsev, a former member of UNPROFOR, deceased in 2008. And we would offer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is Rumyantsev the first or the last name?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2374, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The report or investigation report of this witness and this Russian officer, Rumyantsev, was it admitted in this case or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: He was part of the investigation team whose report is admitted as P1444 -- excuse me, P -- I believe it's P1441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll read out a brief summary of Colonel Moroz's testimony in English now. [In English] Lieutenant-Colonel Sergii Moroz was the mission commander of the engineer section of the Ukrainian Battalion of UNPROFOR in Section Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina, between October 1993 and October 1994. He worked with the Sector Sarajevo headquarters in the PTT building. His unit's main task during that period was to repair and restore utilities such as electricity, gas, and water and sewage. About a month after 5th of February, 1994, explosion which killed many civilians, Lieutenant-Colonel Moroz had a conversation with a Russian officer who had been a member of the UN investigation team which had investigated the shelling at the market-place. His name was Rumyantsev. He told Lieutenant-Colonel Moroz that the explosion was not caused by a mortar launched from the Bosnian Serb side, and that he believed that a special explosive device had been brought into the market-place. Lieutenant-Colonel Moroz visited the Markale market-place. When he visited the scene, he found it strange that a mortar could land in the place where the explosion occurred, given the unusual trajectory required to land a mortar between the high buildings in the area. During his stay at the PTT building, Lieutenant-Colonel Moroz frequently heard mortars being fired from the immediate area of the PTT building. His colleagues from the Ukrainian Battalion of UNPROFOR told him that they had regularly observed mortars being fired from the immediate area of the Marsal Tito barracks in Sarajevo, where they were stationed. The mortars would draw return fire from the Bosnian Serbs close to the UN positions. [Interpretation] That is the summary and at this point in time I have no other questions for Colonel Moroz. I give the floor to the other party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you have noted, Mr. Moroz, your evidence was admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony and now you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, in the summary of your evidence that's just been read out, Mr. Karadzic referred to that part of your testimony in the Galic case regarding what you were told by a Russian officer after the shelling of the market-place in February 1994. In relation to that matter, you said in your Galic transcript that the person that you had an informal conversation with was a Russian military observer or an UNMO called Rumyantsev, that's right, and that's at transcript page 18167. I see you nodding.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that he was part of the team conducting an investigation of the shelling incident and that's at transcript page 18171.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You also said the report was sent to New York, and that's at transcript page 18166.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It was put to you in the Galic trial that a Russian Lieutenant-Colonel N. Rumyantsev had, as part of an investigations team, signed a report which was sent to New York which had findings which were totally contrary to what is alleged he told you. Do you recall that part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I should say that, first of all, I've never seen the official report. I referred only to words of this officer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moroz, so you've never had an opportunity to see this report since you've testified --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P01441, please. And Your Honours at transcript page 18174, there is reference to a Galic Exhibit P2661, which is Karadzic Exhibit P01441.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, the document you see on the screen is an investigations report about the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 13 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see the names, one of the team members as N. Rumyantsev, a Russian UNMO?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see there the signature and signature block Lieutenant-Colonel N. Rumyantsev?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The report states in paragraph 12 just above the signature the nature of the explosion was caused by a conventional factory produced 120-millimetre high explosive mortar bomb which detonated on impact with the ground. The findings also include or indicate the trajectory and the direction from which the shell came - and that's in paragraphs 14 and 15. Do you recall it was put to you that the Prosecution had difficulties in accepting that this person who signed the report with contrary conclusions to what he had allegedly told you was a completely different story? Do you remember that was put to you in the Galic case?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: During Galic case I don't remember that this document was produced to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The document wasn't produced to you; the facts were. And when that was put to you, that the Prosecution had difficulties in accepting the fact that this person who signed the report with contrary conclusions would have told you a completely different story - and this is at transcript page 18173 - you stated that you didn't know if he signed anything at all because you hadn't seen the report and you said that you saw no reason why he would tell you things contrary to the findings of the team's report.

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: -- now I can say the same that everything I told during Galic case about the words of this officer he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that's still your position?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to clarify an answer that you gave in relation to water-supply. At transcript page 18128 to 18129 you were asked about any problems in some parts of the city in terms of supplying water to the civilian population. You said at the bottom of page 18128 and the top of 18129 that sometimes, because there was no electricity, there was no pumping of the water and there was a lack of water in the city. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on page 18129 lines 6 to 10 you said that drinking water was always available in the city but that it wasn't delivered in a normal manner through pipes to their apartments. You said: "The only difficulties for civilians was that they had to 'take water in reservoir and then go upstairs to their apartments so of course it was difficult for many of them.'" Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The use of the word reservoir in the transcript I just read to you, I take it that you're referring to receptacles for carrying water?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Ah, so I meant people went downstairs to ground floor because there -- ah -- so the pressure of the water couldn't afford to go up to higher floors and took in tanks and in some -- anything where water can be put, they took water and went upstairs to their apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The difficulties that you were referring to, though, weren't just the inconvenience of going -- having to go downstairs and get some water lug it back up the stairs --

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- was it?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That was the only difficulty that you saw for the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: It was only one period, two or three days as far as I remember, that it was great shortage of water and trucks with water tanks were going around the old city and people took water out from these tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's the case though, isn't it, that civilians lived in constant fear when they had to venture outside their homes to get food and water?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Of course civilians suffered from the situation when each day there was a risk that water can be cut -- could be cut.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But the water was cut on a number of occasions and the civilians had to risk their lives lining up to get water, did they not?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: So of course it took times and efforts to take water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And sometimes they were queuing up for days in order to get water?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I can't say for this, no, no. Probably one day, yes; two days, I hardly say -- even the two days they couldn't get water. And -- because the next day these tanks with water started driving around the old city and people queuing -- of course queue -- they waited in queues just to get possibility to fill their tanks with water.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And of course that was inherent with risk of being targeted by snipers and shells, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I can't say so because usually these trucks were waiting in safe places where people hardly can be targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check the transcript page in Galic. I can't find that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Neither can I.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could bring it up in e-court. It's on page 16 of e-court of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the page number in hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 18129, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: And the lines, Ms. Sutherland, what lines are they?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 6 to 10, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably I have a different version. Let us see. Why I'm having a different version?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- you may have printed out the earlier version which had been uploaded by the Defence into e-court which was -- had the wrong numbering.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Mr. President. When we uploaded this originally somebody used a word version and the page numbers changed so that was called to our attention and we changed it. So what is currently in e-court is different than what was there previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, you said that the places with -- for the water distribution was normally in safe places, but you know that there were a lot of water distribution points which were out in the open which were easily places where snipers could target markets, trams, and where they were queuing for food?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, of course it was military situation and people always were under risk of being killed, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I can put this to you, Ms. Sutherland, in open session. Do we need to put this transcript provisionally under seal, given the redaction you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That was in open session but it was -- as it was unrelated to the witness I thought it should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just very briefly, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Moroz, today you were told that Rumyantsev said that he did not think that the shell was 120-millimetre shell, although that's what it says in the report. Did you have any information according to which certain UNPROFOR officers were not willing or perhaps couldn't express their personal opinions in public if they weren't in agreement with official reports?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- I object to this question. It's outside cross-examination, and if Mr. Karadzic wanted to ask these questions he could have done it in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This arises directly from the cross-examination because she's confronted him with an inconsistent statement and Dr. Karadzic is seeking an explanation for one reason why that may have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson. Please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moroz, should I repeat my question or do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Please repeat it once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Given that you were shown a report that also bears the signature of the officer with whom you had a conversation, now, did you have any information according to which certain UNPROFOR officers were not willing or perhaps were not even authorised to express some of their beliefs in public if these beliefs diverged from official reports or what was contained in official reports?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: I couldn't say I know definite cases of such kind. I can't neither support nor dis -- so no definite answer here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about water pressure, could you tell the Chamber what such pressure depended on, or rather, what would be the cause of low water pressure and of the fact that water was available only on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: Well, the system of greater part of the city was done in such a way that from water fields near the suburbs of Sarajevo in Ilidza, from that fields engines pumping water on the hill, the place called Mojmilo, where a big water tanks were installed. And from these water tanks, water goes down to the city. First reason of water shortage and low pressure of water in pipes was low level of water in Mojmilo tanks. The main reason of that was that water fields -- the area of water fields in Ilidza very often were shelled and some engines went out of order. The same with electricity line which were -- was -- which was damaged and engines without electricity wouldn't work. For reparation of both electricity lines and engines, time and spare parts needed. Renovation of those systems usually took one, two, up to three weeks. That is why my department engineer, department officers, regularly, each day, went up to Mojmilo and check water-level in tanks. And usually we opened water for several hours in the morning and several hours at night. Because very often only few of engines were operational and not enough water was pumped into Mojmilo tanks. The second reason of low pressure in the system was the following. On the way from Mojmilo to the city there were several wells where -- they were on Serbian and Muslim side, these wells. And closing these wells also can prevent water coming down from the tank to the city -- Mojmilo tank to the city. And very often my section boss, French officer, after checking these wells -- after the signal that no water in the city, checked the -- these wells, and very often one of them was closed. And each time it was the other well. Mostly, as far as I remember, mostly closed the wells were on Muslim side. And among -- in our section among officers we were surprised and even designated [sic] that somebody closed wells and deprived people from water.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question, Colonel. You mentioned that the wells on Ilidza were shelled. On whose territory were those wells and who was it who shelled the wells and the transformation stations there?

utterances.speaker: SERGII MOROZ
utterances.text: These facilities were on Serbian side and so shelling was done from Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for having come here to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Colonel Moroz. On behalf of the Chamber I also would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you brief us on the order of witnesses for the week, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The next witness is Milorad Dzida. He's prepared to begin his evidence today and I was told that the Prosecution is prepared to cross-examine him and we appreciate that very much. Tomorrow -- we don't have any other witnesses for today, and I don't know if he will take the whole day but -- it depends on the Prosecution's cross-examination because the direct examination will be as usual. Tomorrow we will have the testimony of Momir Garic and we don't have any other witnesses after him, and again I don't know exactly how long his testimony will take but it will be mostly a very short direct examination again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see how it evolves. Is the -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may be excused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Let us bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Dzida.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to remind myself and I have to ask you to make a break between questions and answers for the benefit of the interpreters. Please, can you tell me what was your rank when you were pensioned off from the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I was a major when I was dismissed from service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6104 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, did you provide a statement to the Defence? Was that statement read out to you in the Serbian language so you could understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it the statement that you see on the screen and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it accurately reflect what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. If I were to put the same questions to you today in the courtroom in lieu of the statement, would your answers be identical?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender the package into evidence. There is one associated document accompanying the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that it has been signed by the witness and the witness also confirmed it, but I'm wondering why this has the bearing that it is a draft translation? What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the way we received it from CLSS. It's an official translation but this is what -- how we received it. So perhaps we can inquire from them whether they would like to finalise that translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is the original, English or B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any B/C/S version for this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the English is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then why do we have "draft translation"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because we added to this document some additional information and there wasn't enough time to do that in Serbian and then have it translated again since it was done after the proofing. So the document is the original translation from CLSS plus the additional information that was added by our team in the additional paragraphs right before the acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't still follow in full, but do you have any objection, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you're tendering one a document which is 65 ter 8279 as an associated exhibit. You do not have no objection to that either?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both of the -- both of them will be admitted as next Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter number 1D06104 will be Exhibit D2375 and 65 ter number 08279 will be Exhibit D2376.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read a short summary of Major Dzida's statement in English. [In English] Milorad Dzida was a company commander in the 216th JNA Brigade in Han Pijesak. On 19 May 1992 the brigade was renamed to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. On 19th of August, 1993, he was transferred to the 7th Hresa Battalion as assistant commander for intelligence and security. On 17th of October, 1994, he was appointed battalion commander in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. Several years before the war there was already an increasing number of ethnically motivated incidents. During 1990 until 1992, he could not see paramilitary units on Ilidza which the Muslims had already formed in the whole Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. It was well-known that members of Patriotic League and the Green Berets were regularly trained in a secret location at the foot of Trebevic. Upon mobilisation, Muslims in his battalion immediately separated and grouped themselves. They did not want to share tents with the Serbs or take orders from the superior officers unless they were Muslims. Response to mobilisation was also very poor and the Muslims mainly boycotted it. SDA representatives came with the buses and called on all Muslims from the battalion to return home. All Muslims, about 400 of them, left their weapons and went back home. On May the 3rd, 1992, the brigade was sent to Han Pijesak -- sent from Han Pijesak to the Sarajevo sector to Grbavica with the goal of ensuring the unhindered pull out of JNA units from the barracks in Sarajevo which had already become a target of attacks of paramilitary Muslim forces and the Territorial Defence. Firing positions of the 120-millimetre and 82-millimetre mortar batteries on the 7th Hresa Battalion were in the sector of Debelo Brdo and Mrkovici, with three pieces in each firing position. Muslim forces often used sniper fire against the Serb positions, firing at the motor vehicles -- civilian motor vehicles that -- which were used to route -- the route that went through the zone of responsibility of this battalion. The line of Muslim forces were not far -- very far from the lines of his unit's defence positions and it deliberately went through the residential areas inhabited by Muslim civilians, which is why Mr. Dzida's unit often did not return fire. The battalion fired only in situations when they spotted the firing positions of the enemy who was opening fire on them at that point. Fire was never opened on civilians or civilian buildings. The battalion had strict orders to observe every cease-fire and truce. The Muslim side did not observe the cease-fire and his unit was often attacked while the situation was in place, as was the case of an attack on May 1994 from the direction of Faletici and Zecija Glava, when six Serb soldiers died and other six were wounded. Regarding incident known as G8 which is Markale market-place I, a mixed commission carried out an on-site investigation. On 6th of February, 1994, representatives of general headquarter of VRS, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, UNPROFOR, and the 1st Romanija Brigade were taken to the firing positions by the witness, Mr. Dzida. An UNPROFOR commission unexpectedly came to inspect Dzida's unit's positions and mortars. The brigade command informed Mr. Dzida's unit that this UNPROFOR commission would come and inspect their positions in half an hour. The UNPROFOR commission concluded that the mortars were not used for quite some time and that there were no traces of mortar use. In addition, they concluded that the Serb crew did not even approach the mortars recently. A Russian member of the inspecting team measured and calculated the angles around the mortars and had a discussion with the rest of his team. One or two days later a French officer came to Mr. Dzida, battalion commander, and told them that the UNPROFOR had concluded that Mr. Dzida's unit had not opened fire during the Markale incident and gave his belt to the battalion commander Gengo as a present. Milorad Dzida categorically states on the 5th of February, 1994, no shell was fired from those 120-millimetre mortars from any fighting position in the zone of responsibility of his battalion and that those pieces were never moved from their regular firing positions. Just a moment, I think I pronounced something wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to put several questions. I have four brief questions for Mr. Dzida. Before the war did Muslim paramilitaries have training centres only on Trebevic or also elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There was one on Igman and they also went to Croatia to be trained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When did they go to Croatia for training? Did that correspond with the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were sent to Croatia in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your brigade or in your battalion, did you have mobile mortar positions or were those positions as well as targets fixed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In my battalion the mortar positions were stationary and so were the targets that those mortars could aim at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did UNPROFOR visit and inspect your battalion? Were your battalion's positions known to the nearest UNPROFOR team?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Every seven to 15 days our positions were checked and UNPROFOR was familiar with our positions because UNPROFOR was billeted in one part of Mokro which was not very far and they came very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they ever encounter any obstacles to their visits? Were their visits restricted in any way?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: They could visit us freely whenever they wanted to do so without any restrictions. They could come announced or unannounced. So they came and went at their will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, at the moment I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Dzida, as you have noted, your evidence was admitted in the form of a statement in lieu of your oral testimony. And now you'll be

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. If I can have the usher's assistance with the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dzida.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you for meeting with me yesterday, it was very helpful because you and I went over a few maps together and as a result we will save quite a bit of time today. In your statement you indicated that in early May 1992 your unit was sent from Han Pijesak to Sarajevo. And in paragraph 14 of your statement you described the line upon which your unit was deployed. And so yesterday we spoke about that particular line and I gave you a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the ELMO is working.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think I can just do the maps later and over the break they'll be uploaded and we'll do it on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dzida, we're going to come to the maps a little bit later, but nonetheless in paragraph 14 you talked about where your line was deployed and you put that out -- and you mapped that out for me and that was a line in the Jewish cemetery; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in paragraph 15 you spoke about another line of Defence because in August of 1993 you moved units and you went to the 7th Battalion, which is an area north of Sarajevo. And we also later will see a line that you drew outlining that line of defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now also in paragraph 5 of your statement you say in August of 1993 you were transferred to the 7th Battalion to the post of assistant commander - this is paragraph 5 - assistant commander for intelligence and security. And it appears in that paragraph you were in that post for over a year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your role was as a security officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Co-operation with UNPROFOR and co-operation with the troops on the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "co-operation with the troops on the line," be a little bit more specific than that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I toured my men on the line and I provided them with assistance if any was required.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have e-court, please, P04478.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of the rules of service of security organs in the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And we have -- it's a lengthy -- or it's about 33 pages and I'm not going to go through it, but through this document - I suspect you've not read it recently - but through this document it notes a number of the tasks of security officers and part of those tasks - and this would be on page 7 but I don't think we need to go there - is the detection, tracking, and prevention of intelligence activities, is that familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Gathering, verification of information for operational needs, was that also one of your other tasks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And organisation and maintenance of the security organ's information system for purpose of analysing data and intelligence and reporting and informing of that information, was that another task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. It regards analysing data and intelligence and reporting that up your security chain. Was that something you did as well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as regards that chain you had two reporting chains - is that correct? - one to your battalion command but also one to the security command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I reported to the commander and to the chief of the security in the brigade command. I reported to my superior commander in the battalion and the chief of security in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think that makes sense. Part of your other tasks as well would have been the detection and prevention of serious crime, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I wasn't involved in that. We had no such thing in the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you mean you had no crime in the battalion or you weren't involved in that as part of your task?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There was no crime in our battalion which was responsible for protecting Serbian villages. There were people from those villages who were defending their houses, Mrkovici, Gornji and Donji Kresa [phoen], Luke, and so on. They were only defending their families.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I understand what you mean, but one of your tasks, had there been crime committed by your colleagues in the military, that would have been one of the things that you had to look into; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Well, the commander or the chief of security would probably have ordered me to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now you said earlier that you reported to your superior command in the battalion and the chief of security in the brigade. My question is: Why is it so important to have this dual system of reporting? You're reporting to two separate posts. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The chief would give me advice, whereas the commander would issue orders to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you say "the chief," you mean the security chief; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You would also be informing the security chief of information that you learned that you thought might be important for somebody above you to know; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let me ask it again -- in a different way. Part of the reason that intelligence and security information by its nature is so important is that it's something that needs to be known at higher levels than yours; would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Well, for the security of the men and for the security of the lines, it is necessary to provide information to the command, to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have P00191.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's just talk a little bit more about the issue of crime. And you said earlier that would be -- something that in this case you didn't see but that was something that was part of your tasks. What we're going to see in a moment -- these are the guide-lines for determining criteria for criminal prosecution. Sir, if you had become aware that a member of your unit had committed a crime, what was your obligation as a security officer as to whether to report it or not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I'd informed the commander and wait for orders or further instructions as to what to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you had an affirmative obligation to report on that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in front of us we see page 7 in the English, 11 in the B/C/S, of an example of certain criminal offences. And in this example the guide-lines speak in the third paragraph to crimes against humanity and international law. And it says: " ... can be committed by individuals acting on their own, but by their nature these criminal offences are usually committed in an organised fashion in the implementation of the policy of the ruling circles." And it goes on to talk about criminal offences, giving an example of acts against a civilian population. And if I can -- if we can just turn to the next page, please, page 8 in the English, and I'm just going to read a short paragraph. And this regards what we just spoke about, your obligation. It says: "If officers merely find out that units of the armed forces of the Army of Republika Srpska or their members have committed or are committing such acts and take no measures to prevent the consequences or the acts themselves and expose perpetrators to criminal prosecution, this in itself makes them answerable for these criminal offences." Sir, if you merely knew that someone had committed a crime, you had an obligation to prevent or expose them and you did not, you yourself became answerable to that offence; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I have said that there were no such cases in my battalion. I know that I would have prevented any attempts to act in an incorrect way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And we understand that from your earlier testimony, but I just want to know if you agree with this principle that had there been crimes and you knew about it and you did nothing about them, then you yourself could be liable for those crimes according to the guide-lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In this courtroom we've recently been discussing the shelling at the market-place in February of 1994, and I will continue to talk about that with you momentarily, but there's several paragraphs in your statement that regards events preceding February 1994. And there's one of them that I want to touch upon that jumped out at me and Mr. Karadzic actually asked some questions about it. In paragraph 7 of your statement you said: "During 1990 ..." I'll give you a moment to get there. Paragraph 7. "During 1990" and "1992, I could not see paramilitary units on Ilidza which, as it was later found out, the Muslims had already formed in the whole BH by that time." So just to be absolutely clear, when you say you could not see paramilitaries in Ilidza, you mean Bosnian Serb paramilitaries; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I had Muslims in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether the witness said "we saw them in town" or "we did not see them in town."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Then I don't understand. So as to this paragraph you speak about seeing the Patriotic League and the Green Berets regularly training in Trebevic, but when you speak about Ilidza and not seeing paramilitaries, do you mean you didn't see Muslim paramilitaries or you deny ever seeing Bosnian Serb paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Muslim paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And did you see Bosnian Serb paramilitaries in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There were no troops of any kind in Ilidza at the time, but there were the Green Berets and the Patriotic League that were being trained below Trebevic and Igman. Moto Igman was the base for training. My colleagues who worked with me went there for training, my colleagues of Muslim nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. "There are no troops of any kind in Ilidza," so I think I understand this to mean that there were no SRK troops in Ilidza nor were there any Bosnian Serb paramilitaries in Ilidza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In 1992, yes, the SRK, but not around 1990 -- in the 1990s. That's what your question was about.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, my question was about during 1990 until 1992 - which is what your statement says - and what I'd like to know is during 1992 did you ever see any Bosnian Serb paramilitaries in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever heard of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I've heard of him through the news, but I never saw him. In 1991 I left Ilidza and did not return to Ilidza until the end of the war. I only passed through Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Have you ever heard of Legija?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of Brne Gavrilovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Sometimes during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you understand him to be a paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 22235, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I know you said that you were in and out of Ilidza during those years. Have you ever heard of the name Zeljko [sic] Prstojevic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I'll represent to you that he was a political figure in Ilidza and he testified here in this case and another case, and he gave some information about this subject matter and I'd like to look at that. This is previous testimony. And on this page in front of us he was asked: "Did various paramilitary" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm wondering what the purpose is of pursuing this since the witness says he doesn't know the man and he hasn't been to Ilidza, he didn't go to Ilidza. So how would he know anything about what he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, that's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in this testimony he was asked: "Did various paramilitary units come to Ilidza in April and May of June 1992?" And his answer was yes. And on the next page he answered in a more fulsome manner and he said: "Well, I don't know why this is important at the moment. One of those groups is mentioned at the beginning of the intercept. It's Brne's group. Some others like Bokan came to Ilidza for a short while as well as some Chetniks from Zvornik from Republika Srpska, and there are also some groups that simply went in and out of Ilidza. Even Arkan's group spent two or three days in Ilidza." And little bit further down on this page he says: "Brne's group, they were resubordinated to the MUP." As I said, this witness then testified in this case and he was asked about this particular testimony and he -- at transcript 18324 he didn't deny it but he said this: "I didn't work with any of these people, I never asked for any of these people, and as a rule they came on their own free will as an evil." Now you have told us that you were in and out of Ilidza during that period of time, and looking at your original statement, the first one we got, it would suggest your -- you assert that in 1992 there were no paramilitaries in Ilidza. I wonder after hearing this information, does it jog your memory at all as to whether you ever saw or heard about paramilitaries in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I left Ilidza in 1991. I went to see some friends on occasion in February 1992, and after that I didn't go to Ilidza again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So my answer [sic] is: Did you ever see or hear about paramilitaries in Ilidza, notwithstanding your in-and-out nature?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I did not see them nor did I hear about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move on? But before doing that I will confirm with the witness myself. Shall we show him the paragraph 7 of his statement. Mr. Dzida, this is what you stated to the Defence and which was admitted in this evidence in lieu of your testimony. I'll read out the first sentence of this paragraph, 7. Do you understand English, Mr. Dzida?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I'll read it to you. "During 1990, until 1992, I could not see paramilitary units on Ilidza which, as it was later found out, the Muslims had already formed in the whole BiH by that time." So here you referred to paramilitary units on Ilidza. Did you mean Serb paramilitary units or Muslim paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this statement I said in 1990 up until 1992 I didn't notice paramilitary units on Ilidza. So it says up to 1992. 1992 isn't taken into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, my question was whether you meant Muslims or Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Muslims. At the time the Serbs didn't have any units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, when you were interviewed for the first time - so not two days ago, when the original statement was produced - where did that take place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: At Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how many people were in the room during the interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Who were the three?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Two investigators and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What were the names of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Slobodan Batinic was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And who was the other?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The other one was Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you know either one of those investigators before that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: To an extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, when was the first time that you met Slobodan Batinic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us about -- when you say "to an extent," how is it that you knew him?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: We wouldn't meet each other often, but when we did bump into each other we would greet each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, how many years back is the first time that you met Slobodan Batinic? Was it two years ago? Ten years ago? More than that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Perhaps several years ago, perhaps a number of years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry to be so persistent, but "several" and "number" have many different definitions. Can you give us an approximate number of years?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- the witness said "perhaps several years ago." Perhaps more years ago than that, so the interpretation wasn't correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'll just ask you again. How many years ago did you meet Slobodan Batinic for the first time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. A number of years ago we met at some celebration.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During this interview, did you -- was it recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Well, a transcript was made.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So does that mean, yes, it was recorded, or as you were speaking a transcript was being produced on the spot?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: A transcript was produced.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In answer -- the first answer, line 20, the witness said: What we have was produced on that occasion. It means the statement is a result of what was written at the time but it wasn't interpreted correctly. We have problems today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question was whether it was recorded, and then I don't think we had the answer for that question. Could you ask again, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, was the interview recorded?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The gentleman made a transcript and later read it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So are we to understand that as you spoke the transcript was being typed and there was no recording; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes. A transcript was written. It wasn't typed out. It was later typed up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So that -- was that person handwriting on paper as you spoke?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at a later date, were you able to review the typed transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many days later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, just give us the sense as to whether it was within a week or was it months later?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Not a lot later. Before I got my passport out I received the transcript from the meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mumbled at the end of his answer and the interpreter isn't sure he heard him correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask this again because I don't think your answer was responsive. You say: "Not a lot later." But how much later were you able to review the typed transcript? Was it a short time or a long time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Perhaps a week later or ten days later. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when you reviewed the transcript were you given an opportunity to make any corrections to it? Were you given the opportunity to change the words if you thought that that isn't what you had actually said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It accurately reflected what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So the reason I ask this is we've now just come to the first occasion in this statement where it's -- the word usage is quite ambiguous. And then when you came two days later we have further ambiguity resulting. And so I am wondering how is it that when you took a statement whenever you did, months ago, we now have a statement that ends up being quite different and testimony that is coming out to be quite different. Can you give us a reason as to why there is a difference?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we be provided with somewhat more precision as regards these ambiguities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it will be forthcoming. Could you refrain from intervening at the moment. Let's proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, your original statement that we've just spoken about has some issues of clarity, and we just saw an example of one. And you were just interviewed again two days ago and we received another statement that added six more paragraphs. And in particular it added more information that is quite inconsistent with some of the information you gave before. And what I'm wondering is: What happened in the middle of those two events such that the information is now different? So, for example -- go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The information that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not understand the first part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information was added to the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzida, could you repeat your answer. The interpreters were not able to hear the first part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information that was left out from the first statement was subsequently added to the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Dzida, we'll have a break for half an hour, but you are -- you may be already aware that witnesses are not supposed to discuss with anybody else about his or her evidence -- testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, as I understand it, in the time-period immediately after the shelling in February, you were present for a visit to the mortar units of your battalion in two locations and members from the VRS Main Staff, SRK staff, and at least one UNPROFOR person was there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West, are you not coming to the issue of ambiguity or inconsistency in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I can come back to that several times as we go through the statement itself, but I defer to the Court if you have some questions at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand your question. In your question you said -- or you asked me whether we inspected mortars before the shelling or at least this is the way I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to refer everyone to paragraph 17 of your statement and that's a paragraph that was part of your original statement so it was drafted some time ago. In addition, paragraph 29 of your statement, and this was drafted, I think, drafted two days ago, these two paragraphs involve the same subject matter. Some of the information in these two paragraphs is different, and I want to go through that to make sure that we understand exactly what your evidence is. So my first question is: When were you informed that the mixed commission visit was to take place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour or an hour before the visit took place the brigade command informed by commander, who then appointed me as the team leader, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And that information we see reflected in paragraph 29, but let's focus back to paragraph 16, please. And there you say on February 5th, which is the day of the incident, "in the afternoon the brigade command informed us that the incident occurred and that a mixed commission would come to the battalion on that or the following day to carry out an on-site investigation." So, sir, this is one of those occasions that we spoke about earlier where the information is different. And you gave us a reason on page 36 a short time ago, that the reason it was different was the information left out from the first statement was subsequently added to the second statement. But here that's not the case at all. The information is different entirely. Can you tell us why that is?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: As far as I know, that morning when that commission arrived, on that very morning I had been informed that I would be the guide or the team leader and that's when I learned about the Markale incident. I didn't know anything about that beforehand. Maybe this was erroneously transcribed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Well, we can look at the B/C/S, but as regards the English transcription in 16 we have you learning about this commission on the day of the event, but now you're telling us that they unexpectedly showed up at your positions two or three days after the incident. So tell us right now at this moment what is your independent recollection of when you found out they were coming and when they came?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: They arrived on the 6th. They were announced perhaps half an hour or an hour before they actually arrived. We learned that from the command and we set out on the inspection visit from the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And setting out for the -- setting out for the inspection from the command is reflected as that in paragraph 17, but in paragraph 29 it appears that you were already at the mortar position and you didn't have to set out at all. Can you tell us now what at this moment is your recollection as to whether you were already at the mortar position when they came or you were at the battalion command when you heard of it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: At the battalion command, and I went with them in a vehicle belonging to the brigade perhaps. There was a vehicle with Serbian officers, we went to the position, and the UNPROFOR followed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you gave this statement several months back and they transcribed it on the occasion but then came back, I think you said ten days later, for you to review it to make sure it was accurate, did you see this part in paragraph 16 and 17 that is inconsistent with what you're saying right now? Did you say to them: This is wrong, this isn't what I said?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Maybe that was erroneously interpreted or translated to you, but as I've just told you I have ...

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I don't want to cut you off, but I understand that you say that the B/C/S version is probably correct and it's perhaps that the English translation ended up being wrong; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: This is how I see things. Either things have been erroneously translated or your questions are wrong. I apologise. I'm a soldier. I'm not a legal expert. I'm not a lawyer. But you're putting wrong questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at 65 ter 24012, please. And we'll continue to talk about these mortar positions. In paragraph 17, so this is the statement from many months ago, you talked about taking them to two locations of firing positions where the team examined the mortars. And then you give us more information. But we're going to stop there because yesterday when you and I spoke I showed you a map. If we could zoom in -- if we can focus in on the two areas with three little dots. I asked you to put the position of the mortars, because in paragraph 15 you said the firing positions of the 120- and 82-millimetre mortar batteries were in two places. In Mrkovici you had three pieces and in Debelo Brdo you had three pieces. Do you see those two locations here on the map in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not sure -- does the witness have -- no, I believe he does. I wonder if we might be able to zoom in a little bit closer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So now you'll have the opportunity to write on the screen, and we can circle which three are the Mrkovici mortars and which three are the others. You can take that pen and if you can for me circle the three that are Mrkovici, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Put an M --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: This may not be very precise, but I have encompassed them.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Can you put an M next to that, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now circle the three mortars that are at Debelo Brdo, please.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And put a D on that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you sign it and put the date, it's November 1st.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we have a number for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P5952.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday when we spoke you told me that two of the mortars at Debelo Brdo were 120-millimetres and one was 82; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also said as regards the Mrkovici mortars, two of those were 120 and one was 82; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So this is a total of six. I now want to look at paragraph 28 of your report and this is additional information you gave a couple days ago. And in that paragraph you say you'd like to add that in our unit we had two 120-millimetre mortars and two 82-millimetre mortars and none of these four mortars were aimed towards the city. Okay, so this is a total of four mortars. Are these four mortars in addition to the six you showed me on the map or are these part of the six that you showed us on the map?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Those mortars were reported to UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR knew about them. We didn't have any other. I left out one 82-millimetre one probably by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Just so we are completely clear, this talks about four mortars. On the screen you talked about six. Are these four part of those six or should I understand that there's a total of ten?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Please, there were four in one position and another four in another position. In each position there were two 120-millimetre ones and two 82-millimetre ones, and that applied to both positions. I left out one 82 -millimetre one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So I think this could be a translation. Paragraph -- excuse me, line 15 you said there were four in one position and four in another position, but on the map we saw three in one position and three in another position. Do you mean four or three?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And of the four at Mrkovici, how many were 120?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And of the four at Debelo Brdo, how many were 120?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in regards to paragraph 28 you talk about four mortars and you said that none of these were aimed at the city. So now we have got a total of eight mortars I think from looking at what you've said and four not aimed at the city. Were the other four aimed at the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: All the mortars were aimed at the enemy positions. Some of them against one part of the line and the others against the other part of the line. The azimuth was set. The crew was not well trained and they did not have to move the mortars too much because the two lines - ours and theirs - were very close to each other; and they opened fire only on prior approval after an enemy attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's try this again. Were any of those mortars aimed at the city? You told us they were aimed at enemy positions. Were any of those positions in the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No. All of them were outside of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So from your position, north of the city, all of them were either to the east or to the west, but none of them pointing in a southern direction towards the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph 18 you talked about those mortars and -- being fixed and I think we just sort of covered that a bit as well. Mr. Karadzic asked about this during his questions, whether there were any mobile mortars in your battalion. Can you tell us just to be sure, were there any mobile mortars in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In my battalion there were none. They were all stationed in their own positions in Mrkovici and Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So there were no mobile mortars in your battalion but there were mobile mortars in Mrkovici and --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But there were mobile mortars in Mrkovici and Debelo Brdo but they just did not belong to your battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It is not correct. There were no mobile mortars. Those were the two positions and mortars were there stationed from day one to the last day, to the day on which they were all withdrawn from those positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless you know -- I'm sure you know a bit about mobile mortars. And can you confirm for us that they are generally able to move easily and assemble with relative ease?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There were crews on mortars, but they were not a hundred per cent well trained and they could not work with mobile mortars. That's why they were stationed. They had their firing positions and targets on the enemy lines --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch the last part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in case of their attack.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's not responsive to my question. My question is more general. In regard to mobile mortars, are they generally easy to move and assemble?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I really don't know, believe me. In our defence sector, we did not have any mobile mortars. I'm talking about the defence sector of my battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, you only went to your battalion in 1993, as I understand it. So you started off, as I understand it, in 1990. So there must have been some occasion when you were exposed to mobile mortars. Can you tell us whether they're easy to camouflage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I can't speak about something that I didn't do. I was in the battalion from 1993 to 1994, from [as interpreted] the 17th of October.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, at paragraph 17 you speak about the site visit from the commission, and you say that the team, the commission, examined the pieces in detail. They measured the azimuth, made some calculations, spoke with several soldiers from the 120-millimetre crew, and I heard the words of the interpreter who was on the team that it was not possible that fire had been opened from those pieces the day before. Tell us exactly what they did to determine that there had been no firing the day before, and that would be the 5th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I think that in January a cease-fire was signed. We adhered to that cease-fire. The weapons were cleaned and covered. When we arrived at the weapons, one could see that they hadn't been used in a long time. They uncovered the weapons, they looked at the barrels, they measured the azimuth. I believe that a Russian officer did that with the assistance of the others. Then they measured everything and then they agreed that no fire had been opened from that position, and I claim with full responsibility that that's what they stated or at least that's how things were interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On line 8, page 45, "until the 17th of October" and not "from the 17th of October, 1994."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So you've just -- you mentioned here that they were cleaned and covered and you had said that we had adhered to the cease-fire, and this is something that you and I spoke about yesterday. You told me that there was -- that there had been a cease-fire since the beginning of January; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I claim that and I have just repeated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. So during that time there was no shooting from SRK positions into BiH territory or into the city; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have P01562.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's look at the day before, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: P01562 and I think maybe he might be switched over.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is dated February 4th. It's about 10.53 at night. This is an UNMO reporting. This is the evening before. And in the middle it says: " ... BiH in during this period - 64 mixed, 14 AAA. No BiH outgoing heard or seen. BSA outgoing - 8 mixed," and I think it says "50 AAA. Two explosions heard but could not be placed on either BiH or BSA side of confrontation line." Now, this is just the evening before in which we are seeing shells coming into the BiH territory and shells going out of the BSA territory. This truce that you speak of, was this truce ongoing on the day before, on February 4th?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I claim that that truce was ongoing even thereafter, and no single shell was fired by my battalion because there was no need to fire any.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But we're not just talking about your battalion. You had confirmed to me that it was a cease-fire and I said there was no shooting from SRK positions into BiH or the city and you said no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
