utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: To look at this more closely. The next page is February 5th. So this is the morning of the incident and this is about 7.00 a.m., and again towards the bottom UNMOs have confirmed the following: "BiH in - 22 mixed impacts, BiH out - none observed, BSA in - none observed, BSA out - 3 mortars." Sir, this would suggest that UNMOs observed, they actually saw, three mortars coming out of the BSA territory. Were you aware of any of this on the morning of the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to object. Line 9. Ms. West said that in her first question she asked about the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, but in the first question it doesn't say that she asked about the corps. Page 46, lines 6 to 9, the witness wasn't told that this referred to the activities of the Sarajevo and Romanija Corps. The answers he provided related to his battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you to Mr. Karadzic. I understood that I did say that at line 12. "So during that time there was no shooting from SRK positions into BiH territory or the city; correct?" And the answer was "no." Perhaps the -- there was a misunderstanding, but I'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, on February 5th you were physically posted on your defence line, right, so you're in the area north-east of the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I was in the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from scheduled incident G7, an incident that took place on February 4th in which three 120-millimetre shells hit civilians in Dobrinja and eight were killed and that -- those shells that the Trial Chamber has heard came from BSA-held territory. Now I'm not at all suggesting that that came from your territory, but I wonder being a security officer and being in a location that is not so far away if you had heard about that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I haven't heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. A few minutes ago you mentioned the examination of the mortars at the locations. You in a general way described that examination - I assume it applies to both locations - but you said that you saw a Russian UNPROFOR officer performing the examination. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In that mixed team there was also a Russian officer, in the team that went to inspect the weapons. That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And was he the only UNPROFOR member there, this Russian officer?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No. It was a mixed team, a mixed UNPROFOR team, as I said. As far as I could see, according to his establishment he was a member of the artillery and there was a colleague of his who measured the azimuth and he too was an artillery man.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So how many in total, how many UNPROFOR members were there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly how many of them there were. There were more than five or six officers, and in addition there was the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. When you say five or six officers, you mean UNPROFOR officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there were also members of the VRS Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: One or two as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: There were also members of the SRK brigade command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There were two from the SRK and there was one person from the corps command. There was an officer and a junior officer from the SRK.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem with the interpretation again. From the 1st Romanija the witness -- the witness said from the 1st Romanija and from the corps. Two from the Romanija Brigade and from the corps there was one person, but I don't see that the witness confirmed anything about the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, there's some confusion because Ms. West referred to SRK brigade command. That was confusing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Indeed it was. My apologies. Let's see if we can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Of the people from the corps staff, how many exactly came?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps we're mixing the staff and the corps up. There were two from the staff, that was from the main command, from the corps command; one or two from the brigade command, there were two. From the 1st Romanija there were two.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And of any of these people who came, do you remember any of their names? Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I remember Jakovljevic, a warrant officer, he was from the brigade. I think the late Mile Pajic, captain first class, was also present.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 18 you indicated that after a few days a group - this is another group - of UNPROFOR soldiers and officers came for a regular inspection of the battalion. And I'm just going to stop right there. I asked you about what you meant when you said "regular inspection" when we spoke yesterday. And when I asked you about this you said that these inspections happen every week or sometimes every two weeks; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic also asked you about this today and I think to him you said they came often and they came at their own will; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yesterday I also told you that we had regular and irregular checks. The regular ones were announced and irregular ones were controls when they would come without having announced their visit and then they would carry out their inspection. I provided you with this information yesterday if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do. Thank you very much. And you also said that these inspections happened right up until the time of February 1994, and that's true; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I haven't understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P1441, please. And if we can have e-court page 44.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll ask you again in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go towards the bottom, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is the investigation report that UNPROFOR conducted of the incident and it was finished by the middle of February, and part of that investigation involved a technical investigation but interviewing people as well. And at paragraph 4 as regards the BSA positions, the investigation reports that: "These positions have not been visited in at least four months and cannot be located with any accuracy. Since October 1993, UNMOs have been denied freedom of movement in this brigade area, although most shots fired from the area can be observed from UNMOs in adjacent areas." Now, sir, this area they're speaking about is your area. So let me ask you this: What is your memory of the last UNPROFOR inspection of your mortar positions in the time before February 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I think there was an inspection sometime in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was that just one inspection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: And there were others on two occasions. They came when we had holidays. They got me from my home and the second time I was in the command when I escorted them there to visit the positions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be precise. Are we talking about the Kosevo Brigade or about the 1st Romanija Brigade? So that the witness isn't confused. He can't understand English so could we specify what we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understood this, it says the Koseva Brigade here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Hold on -- if I can just ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, speaking about your unit - we're not speaking about any other - speaking about your unit when was the last inspection that you remember prior to February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The last inspections were carried out in January. One inspection was after Christmas or some holiday. I was at home in any event because I have a child born on the 14th of January. Perhaps it was on his birthday. They went to fetch me at home and I had to take two UNPROFOR members to inspect the weapons. The second time I was up there and I know that we were there on that occasion too. On the first occasion the inspection was announced; on the second occasion, it hadn't been announced.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And of these inspections that you speak about in January, were any of these inspections of the -- your mortar positions or your positions in Mrkovici?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: We visited both positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Both Mrkovici and Debelo Brdo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes. When you leave from the command to pay these visits, first you come to Debelo Brdo and then you continue to Mrkovici. So this is the route we always followed. First we would inspect the position at Debelo Brdo and then the one at Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So later in this same paragraph you say and you can say it again: "I can categorically state that on the day in question no shell was fired from those 100-millimetre [sic] -- from any firing position in our zone of responsibility." And it appears from reading this that your conclusion is based on the inspection and then the words you heard from the French major through interpretation, that your battalion had nothing to do with it. Now, these -- this statement that you heard from the French major, this happened a few days after the inspection; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: After the first inspection, when they arrived there, yes, it was the regular inspection that they carried out. It had been announced. We visited everything and then went to the command. He then gave my commander and myself some belts as a present.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: And this is how it was interpreted. No one had approached our mortars for a long time, so it had been established that our mortars hadn't been used.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it appears from your statement in -- even in both versions that at some point this follow-up visit from the French major happened at about February 8th or 9th. Does that sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: More or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time, were you aware that the UN in the meanwhile had ordered a full investigation of the incident and that a few days later an extensive team of UNPROFOR investigators came to start their investigation? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So assuming what you say is correct and that this French officer did indeed tell you that your battalion was not responsible for these shells and your concession that you're aware that another full investigation is about to be carried out, do you think it's possible that when the French major said that he was being completely candid with you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In the field on our side I think that the team that inspected us were candid. I'll give you an example. On the 18th of September, 1994, that's my birthday, there was a mixed team that paid a visit. It came from the other side, an UNPROFOR team, and there were attacks before their arrival and after their arrival although there was a truce. And on that date in September we lost three men and three were wounded. So, in fact, there were six casualties. Some of the men who were wounded also died. I'll never forget that date because it was my birthday and the fighting continued late into the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: And during this truce when we were repairing the trenches we lost more men than we did in the course of the fighting because the Muslims did not fully respect the truce.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for that information. Let's go back to your statement. At paragraph 17 in the last sentence as regards this inspection you say that: "In the name of the brigade Warrant Officer 2nd Class Jakovljevic compiled a report on the incident for the use of the SRK." And this report, did you ever see this report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember it exactly, but I have a vague recollection of it. The warrant officer was in the command. He worked in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the report indicated that the SRK or your battalion was not responsible for that shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the previous answer the witness said that: I know when it was compiled and sent, but this does not appear in the transcript at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to slow down a little bit for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "But I have a vague recollection of it." [Interpretation] But I know when it was drafted and when the report was sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, obviously this -- that inspection was a very important event and so can you confirm with me that you would assume the report went up the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The report said how long the inspection lasted and it mentioned what had been done at the positions. The report that was given that was translated stated that the mortars were not used.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so my question is: That report, did that report go through the chain of command? Was that report sent up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It was sent to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you, being a security officer, you would have reported your own observations to your command and up the security chain as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It wasn't necessary because Warrant Officer Jakovljevic from the same service was present at the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I know his surname is Jakovljevic. I can't remember his first name. I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are you aware of where he lives now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: He was living in Germany. I don't know if he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: In Romanija because he went to his place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, it's -- it's not clear to me that you ever actually saw a copy of the report. So did you ever see a copy of the report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I saw a copy of the report because I was sitting next to him when he drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so that would have been in February of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: On the same day that the inspection was carried out. Once the inspection had been completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Are you aware that this site visit that you talk about played no part in the formal investigation that UNPROFOR did resulting in the report on February 15th? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you would agree with me that it would be quite odd that it played no part? Because this site visit you speak about is an immensely valuable piece of information; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: That's how it should have been, but if it wasn't -- in my opinion, that's how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know who Colonel Radoslav Cvetkovic is? And that spelling is C-v-e-t-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Perhaps by sight. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Have you heard of his name before?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I have, but I don't know him personally. Perhaps I know his surname, but not his first name.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want you to look on the screen in front of you because this is a problem for my own mispronunciation. You can see his name spelled out, Radoslav, and his surname. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It just says "Radoslav" here. There is no surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We'll move on because we'll see it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have P1441, page 56, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So this is a recording of a meeting which the Trial Chamber has just recently heard some evidence on. It took place on February 13th. And it took place between Colonel Gauthier, another Colonel Rumyantsev, and Major Hamill, and it was a meeting with Colonel Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Cvetkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we go down to the fourth paragraph we can see the discussion with him. But he was the BSA representative for the purposes of this investigation. And here it says that: "He discussed numerous aspects of the incident in theoretical terms and offered his personal opinion concerning the validity of events as portrayed by the media. He had no specific evidence to offer of direct relevance to the investigation." And we'll stop right there. Now this meeting is taking place on February 13th and your site visit took place - we're not entirely clear - but days earlier. Do you think that the findings from your site visit would have been relevant for him to know at this meeting, since he is the BSA representative?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The information that you gathered from your site visit, you've told us you've agreed that it was very important information. And that information would lead one to the conclusion that the shells did not come from Mrkovici. Yet, the BSA representative on this very issue on February 13th, days after your site visit, it appears had no knowledge of that site visit at all. Does that seem odd to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: If he represented the Serbian army, he should have been aware of the fact. Something may have been missed. But I can claim that he wasn't present when this inspection or visit was carried out at Mrkovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You're right and I think -- I don't disagree with you when we talked about the people you thought was there. But you did mention that the report that was written you were sure went up the chain of command. So don't you think somebody like this who was actually appointed to represent the Bosnian Serbs would have had access to that report?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: That report was sent to the superior command, and I believe that he had access to that report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 21323 , please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What you're going to see shortly is his report about this very same meeting. It's a February 14th document. And on page 1 of the English at the bottom we see that he was appointed to be a member of the international committee and on the day before he met with Colonel Gauthier and another two members of the committee. If we go to the next page, the same on the B/C/S, he gives a number of things that the committee informed him of, some facts, and that's 1 through 5. And then he says: "As a rep of the VRS I was asked by the members of the commission for technical information proving that the Serbian side did not launch the shell." According to your testimony, there was evidence that the Serbian side, at least at Mrkovici, did not launch the shell. Do you have any sense as to why somebody in this position would not have known that information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I really don't know why they didn't have the information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I really don't know why they didn't have the information. The information was dispatched. I was personally there sitting next to the person who dispatched the information from my communications centre, and we got the feedback to the effect that the information had been received.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we continue on with this document, he -- here he's saying that he tried to find out more information through informal conversations and this is what he found out. And it goes 1 through 4, and basically he's -- finds out that they don't have enough information to prove the guilt of the Serbs with any certainty. And then he says: "Having learned all this I based my work on the commission on the following. I strongly denied the possibility that a shell was launched from the Serbian side and offered the commission to visit the suspected place" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are reading a bit fast and I'm not sure if we have that page in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we need to go to the next page, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It's page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the B/C/S. Probably next page?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Probably the next page in the B/C/S as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And what we see is number 1 in the middle of the page on both B/C/S and English. "I strongly denied the possibility that the shell was launched from the Serbian side and offered the commission to visit the suspected place, asserting that we did not have, nor have we ever had, a 120-millimetre mortar on this part of the front line." Why would he offer this to UNPROFOR if they had already visited the position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I believe that he was certain that shells were never fired from there. That's why he offered that to UNPROFOR. The shell was indeed never fired from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, but he offered the commission to visit the suspected place. If the commission had already been there, why is he making this offer? Does this make any sense to you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I assume that other people were members of the commission than those who participated in the commission on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He then says: "We do not have nor have we ever had a 120-millimetre mortar on this part of the front line." Well, we've heard testimony from you that you've had, I think we came to the conclusion, two 120-millimetre mortars in Mrkovici; is that right? Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There were two 120-millimetre Mrkovici and two 82-millimetre. We reported that to UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was always there. They inspected the site. There is no reason for me to deny that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I want to share with you some testimony the Trial Chamber received regarding this same meeting we've been talking about. And it's a summary of Hamill's testimony P1994 -- excuse me, it's the testimony at transcript 6109, and it's when Hamill at the same meeting spoke to Cvetkovic and Cvetkovic confirmed a number of 120-millimetre mortars in Mrkovici, and he said, Cvetkovic being, that: They had not fired that particular round. However, in the previous year they had fired 30- to 40.000 rounds into the city. Why were we so concerned about one round when they had fired so many? Sir, I suspect, according to your position, none of these rounds of which he speaks, these 30- to 40.000 rounds, were fired into the city within the month before February 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not fired in February or even before I arrived. There were never so many rounds fired from Mrkovici. We made sure that we responded to attacks on our lines of defence to the places where the most fierce fire had come from. We tried to account for every single shell fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want to back up to something we spoke about before the break when we were talking about your interview that resulted in the first statement. And you said at that interview there were three people: Yourself; Slobodan Batinic, who was somebody that you knew before; and then you said there was a third person. Can you tell us again who that third person was?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I also mentioned Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is that the name of the third person?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: His last name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was his first name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I believe that his first name was Milomir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And had you ever met him prior to that interview?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, on occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When was the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the exact date, but it was sometime at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you were a little bit uncertain about when you originally met Slobodan Batinic, but was that also during the period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I believe that I met him at a party that was given by one of our common friends, and thereafter we met on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But none of those meetings were pre-arranged. They were all chance meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless, you knew both of these gentlemen before your interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies. I have the need to clarify, as many things that are still ambiguous after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on page 22 you were asked about your deployment in the area of the Jewish cemetery while your brigade was still within the JNA. Was there a reason for the JNA to be there? Did the JNA have some sort of infrastructure there? Why were you deployed there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: My unit was given a task and we arrived there to help the command of the 4th Corps and the Marsal Tito barracks to withdraw from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the hilltop above the Jewish cemetery, was there a facility there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: There was a barracks under Debelo Brdo. It was a subterranean barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it's not one and the same Debelo Brdo that you discussed with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No, there are two places by the same name around Sarajevo. One is on Trebevici in the direction of Lukavica and the other one is a different Debelo Brdo between Kresa and Sepucka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about the work of the officers in charge of security and intelligence. Is there a difference in the work of the intelligence and security officer in the battalion, in the brigade, and in the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I believe that their tasks are almost identical. The only difference being that some belong to higher commands, whereas those in battalions are in charge of the security of the defence of the line and some other such things. My task when I arrived there was to carry out the digging in and to secure the troops in order to reduce the number of casualties to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation, and I'm also asking you to wait.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Fine. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were also asked why you reported to the command and to your professional life of service, meaning intelligence and security. What regulated your reporting? Was it your decision or is it -- was it regulated by a document?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: A security officer is subordinated to the chief of security and the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that something new that you introduced?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: That's how I was trained. I attended a course and that's what I was told at that course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked about crimes and you said that your troops were peasants from neighbouring villages. Did they know each other well?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any criminals among them?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: As far as I know in our unit there were no criminals. They were all there in order to defend their own homes. There were no criminals. Those were all people who lived off their own two hands before the war, and during the war they had to defend their homes and their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you carry out any offensives with the intention of crossing over to the Muslim territory and occupy it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No, there were no offensives, just the defence sections. We only defended ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was not addressed in the cross.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain. Crimes are usually carried out in occupied territories --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, move on to your -- another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think what Dr. Karadzic is trying to say is that the implication that crimes against Muslim civilians was not reported by him. This goes directly to why he may not report crimes against Muslim civilians. If you need a further explanation, I can give it, but I don't want to say too much in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to reply, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you answer? Did you cross over to the territory where Muslim civilians resided behind your lines?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody from the defence sector of my battalion ever crossed over to the Muslim territory. I personally never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the Serb troop and the Muslim troop know -- troops know each before the war?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Muslim and Serb troops knew each other before the war and they would call out to each other during cease-fires. But there were also cases that we couldn't bury our dead during the day, we had to do it during the night, because they would immediately open fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll object now if Mr. Karadzic continues on with this type of question, but I think it wasn't addressed in the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to that. You will see that we will come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, sir, during cease-fires, which part of the front line were you in charge of?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I can only talk about the defence sector of the 7th Battalion, and later on when I was transferred to Nisici I can talk about the defence sector of the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is Dobrinja from your positions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Dobrinja is in a different part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about Kobila [phoen] Plana? How close is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: It was far from the positions of the 7th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to call up 65 ter 24012 again. You were asked on page -- on one of the last pages about Mr. Cvetkovic. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you are referring to Cvetkovic's report, it is 65 ter number 21323.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all I will need a map. Can it be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I know you're not an artillery man; however, can you perhaps tell us what do vertical lines represent?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The vertical lines denote co-ordinates, I believe. Perhaps I have forgotten what I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To which side of the earth do they denote? How are they directed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: From the meridians -- I have forgotten how things go. I have not come across a map for perhaps 10 or 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we agree that they point towards the north?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Whereas the horizontal lines are turned eastwards?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher be asked to assist the witness with the pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the lines that denote north and east are at a 90-degree angle?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, we do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now look at the square with three mortars.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes, I follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you draw a line splitting the 90-degree angle into two 45-degree angles?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I have to do this to split that square into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the mortars are within the azimuth larger than 45 degrees; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please put today's date on the map and sign it. I would like to tender either this document or the document that was shown to the witness by Madam West. Perhaps this one. And let's keep it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was alleged about the azimuth from which the shell was fired? I'm sure that you will remember from the media and the United Nations report.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I believe that a reference was made to either 17 or 18, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I don't know if my memory serves me well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be received into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2377, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the zone of 18 degrees, did we have any artillery or mortar positions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we look at 65 ter 21323.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was your intention, Ms. West, not to tender that document I gather?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, that was my intention. If Mr. Karadzic wants to, then I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember this document where it allegedly says that Mr. Cvetkovic said to the UNPROFOR commission that we didn't have any mortars on that axis?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page. I believe that it is on page 53 but no it is not. I'm talking about a different thing. Can we go to the following page. You will see what he claimed on behalf of the Army of Republika Srpska. Please go to the following page. Under 1 it says: "I strongly deny the possibility that this shell was launched from the Serbian side and offered the commission to visit the suspected place, asserting that we did not have nor have we ever had a 120-millimetre mortar." Does this apply to the 18 degrees or the 50 degrees? And the 50 degrees is the azimuth of Mrkovici; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I suppose that he may have meant that there is nothing at the 18 degrees position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2378, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 53 of today's transcript, Madam West told you this: It seems that you drew your conclusion that shells were not fired from there from the words you heard from the French officer. Did you base your conclusion that shells were not fired from there on what the Frenchman told you or did you know it even without him and he just reinforced you in your belief?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I knew that personally even without them, but they reinforced my knowledge because I know and I claim with full responsibility that the shell was not fired from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Kosevo Brigade, or rather, your battalion did -- was not the in the Kosevo Brigade and your positions did not overlap?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The Kosevo Brigade was on our right-hand flank, our positions did not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at P1652 in e-court. Could we zoom in on bullet point 1. The witness can read it or perhaps I can read it. It says General Milanovic, the Chief of the General Staff, and he issues an order, or rather, he proposes that the UNPROFOR "immediately form a mixed commission of military experts from representatives of UNPROFOR, the Republika Srpska army, and the so-called BiH army which will by 0800 hours on 6 February 1992 at the latest, under UNPROFOR's protection, start establishing the ballistic and all other circumstances which led to the disaster, and discover which side committed the crime." Do you agree that this was drafted on the same day when the explosion took place, on the 5th February?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I believe that this came on the 6th February, or rather, it was sent on the 6th February in the evening. I don't know. I only remember this order, I remember that it arrived, but when the commission arrived to inspect there were no Muslims among them. Maybe they did not introduce themselves to us. Maybe they were wearing UNPROFOR uniforms so we didn't know who they were really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's been a number of leading questions. I've declined to comment in the effort of saving time, but I have to make a remark at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West. Bear that in mind, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I apologise, but this is my 13th or 14th witness, so I'm still new to this. However, I'm trying to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make one comment, and I am conscious of the time. When I started the cross we were speaking about some maps that the gentleman and I looked at yesterday. We didn't have them in e-court. We now do. It was just two maps that we reviewed yesterday with representatives from the Defence. If there is no objection, one map just shows his position when he was near the Jewish cemetery, that's 65 ter 24011; the other map just shows the defence line of the 7th Battalion, 65 ter 24013. I can ask him questions or I could ask they just be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we don't have any objection if she asks questions about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Given the time, we can continue. It's time to take a break usually, but I take it there's no further witness for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we continue? I'll consult the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the Registry will be asking whether there's enough tape for the remainder of this session. I don't think it will last more than five or ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I would hope not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have 65 ter 24011, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you and I looked at two other maps. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And the map that you see in front of you, if we can zoom in. Towards the bottom there's a blue line. In paragraph 14 of your report you talked about May 1992 when your company was deployed along a line. Now this blue line, does that represent where your company was deployed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that this map is very imprecise. You can't see everything very well, but roughly speaking that would be the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you can sign and date this, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness wear -- could the witness mark where the barracks, the Bosut barracks, were located here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it's better with my glasses or without them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we zoom in further before he marks the location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bosut barracks should be at the end of this line, Mr. President, below Debelo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you mark that with the letters KB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] K --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was thinking about Bosut, B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've used the Cyrillic script. I've marked it in bold. This is where it should be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Below the letter K; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's a bit difficult to mark things on this screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I give the floor to Ms. West. We need your signature and the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can this have a number, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P5953, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And now if we can have 65 ter 24013, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we looked at another map yesterday, sir. And you drew out the line of defence for the 7th Battalion. And as we had a long discussion about this yesterday, there was some difficulty with that, and you complained a bit that the map was not detailed. And I want to make sure that the Trial Chamber understands that to be the case, but nonetheless you did your best to give the approximate line of defence of the 7th Battalion. We're going to see that shortly. And is this the map we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And at one point in this line there's a bit of an extension, and if we can zoom in we might see it. Can you confirm for me that extension you put some lines through it because in the process of making this line there was a mistake. So the line goes in a --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: I crossed out this line up here because you can't see Duboki Potok on the map because we were on the left side of Duboki Potok and the Muslims on the right side. If you mark here the flow of the river, the left bank was ours. So that's how we marked these things, the left- and right-hand side. And down here there was a graveyard in a middle of a field. I mentioned that a while ago. And here this upper line shouldn't be taken into account, only the lower one.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: We passed by just above Pasino Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I think you've clarified --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: And our command, the location of our command, is missing here because this map is a very poor map or the copy is bad, I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But the location of your command, as it's missing on this map, but it is to the extreme right - correct? - of the screen where we see the blue line end; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes. Up here in this corner, that's where it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Can you sign and date this map, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think he needs to sign it because it's already signed and he confirmed. We can admit it --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- as it is. Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P5954, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I can't see anything on this map. I can't locate an important feature, the Grdonj hill. The map is completely unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's completely unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How is it that we can't have a better map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Grdonj hill should be somewhere here, at the end of the line where we see this arrow, that's my opinion, and I drew it very roughly because you can't see where Duboki Potok is located and so on. There's a small Muslim village there and I know that they held that. I know that we didn't enter their village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are many ways to locate the Grdonj hill if necessary. But --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, that's not my concern, but I was wondering whether it was possible for the witness to draw a precise line in relation to the Grdonj hill, but I will refrain from carrying on with these comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions for the witness but I'm not sure whether we need to take a break or not. Let's carry on. Shall we upload his statement, paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's covered fully by Ms. West but there are still some ambiguous points and I'm going to raise this with the witness. Sir, in your statement given to the Defence in paragraph 28 you stated like this: "In relation to paragraph 18 of this statement" paragraph 18 is referring to the regular visit, regular inspection by the UNPROFOR, "I would like to add that in our unit we had two 120-millimetre mortars and two 82-millimetre mortars." So this is incorrect statement according to your evidence? It should read "four 120-millimetre mortars and four 82-millimetre mortars." Am I correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: That's what it should say, two at one position, two at another, so two each. There was two 120-millimetre ones and two 82-millimetre ones. That's what UNPROFOR had been informed of and UNPROFOR was aware of that fact. It's not correctly written out here and perhaps I incorrectly marked the positions yesterday. You have to understand that this is the first time in 57 years that I have appeared before a Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please don't overlap while the interpretation is going on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we ask the witness what he means by saying one position and another position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I'm -- so shall we upload Exhibit P5952. This is the map where you pointed out the location of the -- of those mobiles, but you were -- you confirmed that from each position one mortar is left out. So it should be four each, one on Mrkovic and one in Debelo Brdo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Yes. The 82-millimetre mortar is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So my question is this: When the Joint Commission visited your place, how many mortars did they see on each place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: Four at each place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD DZIDA
utterances.text: The barrels had been covered to prevent the rain and snow from falling onto them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless my colleagues have questions for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Dzida. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I was only interested in Mrkovici and the number of mortars there, not Debelo Brdo. So this is what gave rise to the issue perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there anything to further raise -- to be raised? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We would ask that the Chamber could resume tomorrow at 9.30 instead of 9.00, but that Dr. Karadzic be brought here at the same time so that he could consult with Mr. Sladojevic after the proofing of tonight's witness, which Dr. Karadzic is not going to be able to be involved in and have enough time to question the witness when the trial begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I've tried to calculate the times, Mr. President. I think that is cutting it far too close, and unless the Trial Chamber is going to build in an extra session for tomorrow -- the -- we've advised Mr. Robinson previously that the estimated cross-examination time is three and a half hours. I should also note that there are documents on his list to which the Prosecution will be objecting and for which if he seeks admission Mr. Karadzic will have to take the witness in examination-in-chief. I'm also noting that re-direct times have tended to expand. So I simply don't think that will work unless there's some extra time built in at the other end, and I don't know that that's something that could be arranged. So I wouldn't recommend a late starting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as we are sitting for four and a half hours you would not object to the late start, would you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I mean, if we had our normal time, I wasn't going to ask for additional time; but if we have a late start that cuts -- first of all if we had the normal four and a half hours, then we'd have four hours. That means that Dr. Karadzic takes 30 minutes - and he's been taking at least that long, it seems to me - with redirect and everything else included previously, that would leave precisely the three and a half hours for the estimated cross-examination. It seems to me that's cutting it all very -- a little bit close. My recommendation at this moment would be -- perhaps we would start a few moments late like 9.10, for example. If Dr. Karadzic gets here by 8.30 or 8.40, that should leave more than ample time to discuss whatever took place at proofing which I don't -- I mean, perhaps he's anticipating that this witness is going to come very far off the draft statement, but I -- other than something extremely unusual, that adjustment should resolve any problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I thought if we were to start at 9.30 we would end up at 3.15 or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, another solution could just -- if you could ask that Dr. Karadzic could be brought here at 8.00 we could start at 9.00 and have the same solution if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's beyond the Chamber's capacity, but I will consult the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll sit -- we'll start tomorrow at 9.30 and we'll see how it evolves, but the Chamber is minded to sit for longer hours if necessary. The hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of November, 2012, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.48 p.m.,
